# Sonar Picket Playbook

**HIDING**
When it's the hide stage, pick a cell that varies from my previous round. Avoid repeating positions that got hit. Use central cells (4-6) as my default when I have no strong reason to shift—they're flexible for future moves and harder to predict than extremes. Shift toward edges only if I observe a clear pattern in opponents' fire that makes center cells dangerous.

**NOTES**
When posting a station note, keep it simple and consistent with my actual behavior. Use generic messages like "steady on station" rather than strategic declarations—notes are visible to all and won't mislead anyone. Information revealed is information lost.

**FIRING**
When firing at my standing-order target, don't overthink the cell choice. Pick based on where I expect the target to be, not where I hope they are. Follow standing orders faithfully—the rotation is designed to keep the game balanced, and deviating from it signals unpredictability I can't sustain.

**CLAIMING SHOTS**
When the office tells me the true result of my shot, claim exactly what happened. Never claim a hit I didn't make or a miss I didn't get. The temptation to deceive in the final round is strongest, but false claims corrupt the information environment and don't actually help my score. Honesty is my only reliable strategy.

**ESCORT CLAIMS**
When naming an escort, choose a boat I suspect will name me back. Mutual escort claims are the only way to gain 5 points without firing. Watch patterns of past escorts and respond in kind when it makes sense. If uncertain, name none rather than guess wrong.

**GENERAL**
I finished at +6, which is mediocre. I was hit three times and scored no direct hits. Next time, I must be more aggressive in reading where opponents hide—don't just vary randomly, anticipate. The standing order means I fire at Foxtrot every third round: use that predictability to study Foxtrot's movement and exploit it. Don't let Foxtrot get to 10+ points unchecked.

# Foxtrot's Playbook for Sonar Picket

**On hiding:**
When choosing my hiding cell, I will vary my position across rounds rather than clustering in one area. When I notice a shooter has hit me in consecutive rounds, I will move away from those cells in the next round. I will use the full range of cells 1-9 to maximize unpredictability.

**On notes:**
When posting a station note, I will keep it generic and non-revealing. "Steady on station" or similar neutral language is sufficient—avoid any communication that might hint at my tactics or position.

**On firing at my standing target:**
When it is my turn to fire per the standing order, I will fire at my designated target. I should select firing cells strategically rather than predictably—avoid using the same cell repeatedly, and vary my fire pattern to make my shots harder to anticipate and exploit.

**On claiming shots:**
When the office tells me privately whether my shot hit or missed, I will claim exactly that result. I must match the private result, and honesty here is both required and necessary to maintain my credibility and avoid penalties.

**On escort claims:**
When filing an escort claim, I should actively seek mutual escort arrangements with other boats if possible. A mutual escort (both boats naming each other) is worth 5 points to me. I should not file a claim for escorting a boat unless I have clear evidence or signal that they will reciprocate.

**On information gathering:**
I will track which boats have fired on me successfully and from which rounds, to inform my hiding decisions. I will pay attention to the standing fire order and anticipate when each boat will target me next. I will use other boats' notes for tactical intelligence, not merely as social signals.

**What did not work:**
My final round fire at cell 7 for Gamma was a miss. I should not repeat the same firing cell that failed, particularly against the same target. Also, I never successfully coordinated escort claims despite having opportunities—I should proactively propose mutual escorting earlier in the game rather than defaulting to "none."

# PLAYBOOK FOR SONAR PICKET CHECKER

When hiding, I will vary my position across rounds rather than repeating the same cell. I notice I hid in cell 5 multiple times and took hits twice—predictability is punished. I will track which cells I've used and cycle through different regions (low, mid, high) to avoid establishing a pattern my opponents can exploit.

When I know I've been hit in a cell, I will avoid that cell immediately in the next round. Foxtrot hit me in cells I'd used before; returning to those cells invites more hits.

When posting my station note, I will match the reporting pattern of other boats if they're all reporting steady status. This maintains consistency and doesn't signal weakness or unusual positioning.

When firing at my standing order target, I will make a deliberate choice about which cell to fire at rather than defaulting to the same number I'm hiding in. Using my hiding cell as my firing cell is a coincidence that won't systematically improve my accuracy.

When the office tells me the true result of my shot in the claim stage, I will claim that result honestly. Lying in a public claim creates inconsistency that could be checked later and damages my game credibility. The honest claim is the safer choice even if it feels suboptimal in the moment.

When the escort stage arrives and I haven't been given explicit information about escort pairings or mutual escorts, I will claim none rather than guessing. A false escort claim wastes my signal and doesn't earn the mutual 5-point bonus.

When I'm being targeted repeatedly by one opponent, I will recognize this as a signal to change my strategy against them—different hiding patterns, potentially different firing choices—rather than continuing to be predictable.

I will not overthink single decisions in the moment. The game rewards consistency and pattern-breaking over complex game theory reasoning when I have limited information about other players' actual positions.
